full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: This is a petitioner under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the proceedings of ICT-BD Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2010 pending before the International Crimes Tribunal, Dhaka. 

 2. It has been stated in the petition that the petitioner is the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh. He is an ex-Minister of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. However, on 26-7-2010, upon an application by the Chief Prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal, warrants of arrest were issued against the petitioner and others. On 29-7-2010, the law-enforcing agencies submitted a report to the Tribunal to the effect the warrant of arrest issued against the petitioner could not be executed as he was detained in custody in connection with some other criminal cases. Accordingly by an order dated 29-7-2010, the Tribunal directed the police to produce him before the Tribunal on 2-8-2010. On 2-8-2010, he was produced before the Tribunal passed an order directing the law-enforcing agencies to send him to jail-custody and further to produce him three before on call. The above-mentioned orders of the Tribunal issuing the warrant of arrest against the petitioner on 26-7-2010 and directing the police to produce him on 2-8-2010 are without lawful authority. The Tribunal is not empowered to commence any proceedings or pass any order in relation to the petitioner before submission of any formal charge. The orders of the Tribunal are in violation of the provisions of section 11(5) of the International Crimes (Tribunal) Act, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the Act of 1973). As such, the alleged proceeding of the Tribunal are of no legal effect. 

 3. At the outset, Mr Abdur Razzaq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that he has invoked the inherent powers of the High Court Division as contemplated by section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure with a view to quashing the proceedings of ICT-BD Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2010 pending before the Tribunal in view of the fact that all constitutional remedies available to the petitioner are absolutely barred by the provisions of Articles 47(3) and 47A of the Constitution. 

 4. Mr Abdur Razzaq next submits that regard being had to the provisions of Article 109 of the Constitution and those of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court Division is competent to quash the proceedings of the case pending before the Tribunal; though the Code has been made inapplicable to the proceedings of the Tribunal as provided by section 23 of the Act of 1973. 

 6. Mr Abdur Razzaq also submits that according to Article 94 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court is the apex Court of the country and it has two Division-one is the High Court Division and the other is the Appellate Division and since the High Court Division is an integral part of the Supreme Court, the Tribunal is necessarily subordinate to the High Court Division and that being so, the inherent powers of the High Court Division are available to the petitioner for quashing the proceedings of the case pending before the Tribunal. 

 8. Mr Abdur Razzaq further submits that the High Court Division has the authority to decide as to whether the proceedings of the Tribunal are in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Act of 1973 and if the proceedings of the Tribunal are not in accordance therewith, the High Court Division may intervene in an appropriate case under section 561A of the Code Criminal Procedure in spite of the inapplicability of the Code as envisaged by section 23 of the Act of 1973. 

 11. Mr Abdur Razzaq further submits that although the investigation report is yet to be submitted by the Investigating Agency, but the fact remains that it is the rarest of rare cases and in consequence at this investigation stage, the case can be quashed under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 12. In support of the submissions, Mr Abdur Razzaq refers to the cases of Syed Md Hashem vs State, 48 DLR (AD) 87; Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 38; Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16; Nasiruddin Mahmud vs Momtazuddin Ahmed, 36 DLR (AD) 14; Emperor vs Khawaja Nazir Ahmad, AIR (32) 1945 Privy Council 18; Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal, 3 BLC (AD) 155 and Rana Birpal Singh vs Emperor, AIR (36) 1949 Bombay 161. 

 15. Mr MK Rahman further submits that according to section 6(2) of the Act of 1973, any person who is a Judge, or is qualified to be a Judge, or has been a Judge, of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, may be appointed as a Chairman or a Member of a Tribunal and the incumbent Chairman and one of the Members of the Tribunal are the sitting Judges of the High Court Division and the other member of the Tribunal is qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and as per section 21 of the Act of 1973, the right of appeal against any order of conviction or acquittal passed by the Tribunal lies with the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and this being the state of affairs, it cannot be said that the Tribunal is subordinate or inferior to the High Court Division and as the Tribunal is not amenable to the Jurisdiction of the High Court Division, the instant petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is misconceived. 

 17. Mr MK Rahman further submits that the virus of the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1973 was challenged in Writ Petition No. 6836 of 2010 and ultimately that Writ Petition was rejected as being not pressed on 23-8-2010 and as an after-thought, the petitioner has come up with the instant petition under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to challenge the initiation of the case pending before the Tribunal. 

 18. Mr MK Rahman also submits that being unsuccessful in Writ Petition No. 6836 of 2010, the present petition has been filed by way of a smart trick in view of the Admitted fat that the proceedings of ICT-BD Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2010, amongst others, were also challenged in that Writ Petition. 

 19. Mr MK Rahman further submits that in any view of the matter, the Tribunal is not sub-ordinate to the High Court Division and unless the Tribunal is subordinate thereto, it cannot exercise its inherent powers under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this regard, he has drawn our attention to the case of Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan vs State reported in 13 MLR (AD) 150. 

 20. Mr MK Rahman also submits that the Tribunal has been vested with the power to issue warrant of arrest against the petitioner during the investigation of any case in view of the provisions of rules 6 and 9(1) of the International Crimes Tribunal Rules of Procedure, 2010 (hereinafter mentioned as the Rules of 2010) and he Tribunal did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned orders as such. 

 23. It transpires that Mr Abdur Razzaq has rightly submitted that no constitutional remedied are available to the petitioner because of the provisions of Articles 47(3) and 47A of the Constitution; through the alleged proceedings of ICT-BD Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 2010 were unsuccessfully challenged in Writ Petition No. 6836 of 2010. 

 24. One of the most vital questions that have cropped up in this case is whether the Tribunal is subordinate to the High Court Division or not Part-VI of the Constitution deals with the Judiciary. Chapter-1 of Part-VI deals with the Supreme Court. As per Article 94(1) of the Constitution, there shall be a Supreme Court for Bangladesh (to be known as the Supreme Court of Bangladesh) comprising the Appellate Division and the High Court Division. So it is seen that the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is the apex Court of the country and it has two components-one is the High Court Division and the other is the Appellate Division. 

 26. In the decision in the case of Abdul Mannan Bhuiyan vs State reported in 13 MLR (AD) 150 adverted to by Mr MK Rahman, it has been held in paragraph 18 and 19: 

 28. In the decision in the case of Emperor vs Khawaja Nazir Ahmed reported in AIR 1945 Privy Council 18 relied on by Mr Abdur Razzaq, it has been held that it is not correct to say that section 561A has given increased powers to the Court which it did not possess before that section was enacted. The section gives no new powers, it only provides that those which the Court already inherently possess shall be preserved and is inserted, lest it should be considered that the only powers possessed by the Court are those expressly conferred by the Code of Criminal Procedure and that no inherent power had survived the passing of the Code. 

 29. It is true that the inherent powers of the High Court Division have been recognized by insertion of section 561A in the Code by Act No. 18 of 1923. Be that as it may, after its insertion in the Code, section 561A has become an integral part thereof. It is not an isolated inland. It is very much a part and parcel of the Code. It goes without saying that as per section 26 of the Act of 1973, it is an overriding law. It is in the scheme of the Act of 1973 that the operation of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 and the Evidence Act, 1872 has been expressly ousted by section 23. Because of express inapplicability of the Code of Criminal Procedure to any proceeding before the Tribunal as per section 23 of the Act of 1973, we do not find any earthly reason to hold that the inherent powers of the High Court Division can be called in aid to quash the proceedings of the case, if any, pending before the Tribunal. 

 31. There is no gainsaying the fact that the investigating Agency is still collecting evidence against the petitioner, Needless to say, no investigation report has yet been submitted by the Investigating Agency to the Tribunal through the Chie Prosecutor or any prosecutor, as the case may be. However, from the language employed in section 11(5) of the Act of 1973, it is abundantly clear that unless and until the petitioner is charged with any crime specified in section 3, the Tribunal shall have no power to direct, or issue a warrant for, the arrest of the petitioner, and to commit him to custody, and to authorize his continued detention in custody. 

 32. Rule 6 of the Rules of 2010 contemplates that if the Investigating Officer has reason to believe that any offence has been committed, he shall proceed in person to the spot, investigate the facts and circumstances of the case and if necessary, take steps for the discovery and arrest of the discovery and arrest of the accused. Again Rule 9(1) of the said Rules provides that the Investigating Officer, through the Prosecutor, may obtain a warrant of arrest from the Tribunal for the arrest of a person at any stage of the investigation, if he can satisfy the Tribunal that such arrest is necessary for effective and proper investigation. Upon examining the aforesaid provisions of Rule 6 and Rule 9(1), it is beyond any shadow of doubt that while the investigation is underway, a warrant of arrest may be issued by the Tribunal in an appropriate case to secure the arrest of the accused. 

 34. In the case of Shaheda Khatun vs Administrative Appellate Tribunal, Dhaka and others reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155, it has been held that the Appellate Tribunal seems to be totally unaware of the settled law that notwithstanding the ouster of jurisdiction of the High Court Division by any legislative provision or even under Article 102 itself, the High Court Division is yet entitled to exercise its power of judicial review under Article 102 if the action complained of before the High Court Division is found to be coram non judice, without jurisdiction or taken malafide. 

 35. Undeniably the above law declare by the Appellate Division is binding is binding upon the High Court Division according to the mandate of Article 111 of the Constitution. But it may be pointed out that the case of Shaheda Khatun was a case of judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution and in that case, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was Ammegs found to be coram non judice. In this connection, we feel tempted to say that the power of judicial review has been specifically vested in the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. This is, no doubt, an extra-ordinary power of the High Court Division. Reverting to the present case, in any event, we are not exercising the power of judicial review of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. This being the strikingly distinguishing feature, the reference to the case of Shaheda Khatun reported in 3 BLC (AD) 155 will not be of any avail to Mr. Abdur Razzaq. 

 36. According to Mr Abdur Razzaq, in spite of the inapplicability of the Code of Criminal Procedure as contemplated by section 23 of the Act of 1973, the said Code can be applied to any proceeding before the Tribunal, having regard to the 'ratio' enunciated in the case of Rana Birpal Singh vs Emperor reported in AIR 1949 Bombay 161. In that decision, it has been held that section 491(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not a bar to the High Court's ascertain whether a detention is, in fact, a detention under the Bengal State Prisoners Regulation (1818) and that whether a detention is or not a detention under the Regulation is a matter of substance and is not concluded by the circumstance that the Regulation is mentioned in the warrant. However, the facts and circumstances of that case are quite distinguishable from those of the present case. Against this backdrop, we are not impressed by the analogy between section 23 of the Act of 1973 and section 491(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as argued by Mr Abdur Razzaq. 

 38. Assuming for the sake of argument that the Code of Criminal Procedure is applicable to the proceedings of the Tribunal, only then section 9(1) of the Act of 1973 will come into play. Section 9(1) provides that the proceedings before a Tribunal shall commence upon the submission by the Chief Prosecutor, or a Prosecutor authorized by the Chief Prosecutor in this behalf, of formal charges of crimes alleged to have been committed by each of the accused persons. It is undisputed that no formal charges of crimes alleged to have been committed by the petitioner have been submitted before the Tribunal as yet. In such a posture of things, it is crystal clear that no proceedings have commenced before the Tribunal at this stage. This being the position, can the case be quashed? 

 39. In the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38, the Appellate Division has clearly spelt out the categories of cases where the High Court Division should interfere under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In that decision, the Appellate Division has observed as follows: 

 (a) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on the admitted facts, no case can stand against the accused; 

 (c) Where there is a legal bar against institution or continuance of a criminal case against an accused person; 

 (d) In a case where the allegations in the First Information Report or the Complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence alleged and in such cases no question of weighing and appreciating evidence arises; and 

 (e) The allegations made against the accused person do constitute an offence alleged; but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 40. The above-mentioned categories of cases as spelt out our Appellate Division in the decision reported in 28 DLR (AD) 38 have been subsequently followed in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain reported in 17 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16. 

 41. In the case of Sher Ali vs State reported in 46 DLR (AD) 67, the Appellate Division has held that the inherent power may be invoked independent of powers conferred by any other provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and this power may be exercise to quash a proceeding or even a conviction on conclusion of a trial if the Court concerned had no jurisdiction to hold the said trial or the facts alleged against the accused do not constitute any criminal offence, or the conviction has been based on 'no evidence' or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. 

 43. The Supreme Court has considered the scope of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in two cases reported in 26 DLR (SC) 17 and 28 DLR (AD) 38. The view taken in 26 DLR (SC) 17 case is that the statutory power of the police to investigate cognizable offences cannot be interfered with under section 561A and that section is not be utilized to intercept or obstruct the ordinary course of procedure as laid down in the Code. We have already observed that no proceedings of the Tribunal have commenced in relation to the petitioner till now. Moreover, we are quite in the dark about the contents of the complaint, if any, lodged with the Investigating Agency against the petitioner on the basis of which the investigation has been set in motion. On top of that, it is not 'one case out of a thousand' where the power of quashing can be exercise under section' 561A of the Code at the investigation stage. So the reliance of Mr Abdur Razzaq upon the decision in the case of Syed Md Hashem vs State reported in 48 DLR (AD) 87 does not carry conviction. 

 44. Before parting with the case, we would like to say that another Bench of the High Court Division presided over by Mr Justice Sharif Uddin Chaklader allowed the Tadbirkarak of the petitioner to swear the affidavit dated 26-8-2010. Mr MK Rahman has emphatically submitted that the High Court Division committed a wrong by allowing the Tadbirkarak to swear the affidavit in complete disregard of the inapplicability of the Code of Criminal Procedure as provided by section 23 of the Act of 1973. Anyway, that is a 'fait accompli'. So we refrain from making any observation thereon.
